988.title: Isfahan, half the world
988.hook: the Safavid capital, with its great square and blue-tiled mosques
988.howItsDone: Mosques from Morocco to Indonesia are often decorated with tilework, calligraphy of Qur'an verses and geometric and floral patterns, and a mosque's prayer hall is oriented toward the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Safavids: a Sufi family from Ardabil that took a throne and changed the faith of a country. Your line was: iran becomes shia. Whose different view did you listen to without trying to win? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

The people at the far end of the square look like grains of rice. That is how long it is. Fountains run down the middle. Arcades of shops line every side, and on each side something different waits: a palace with a high porch where the shah could sit and watch, a bazaar gate, and mosques covered in blue. Polo was once played on this ground, with goalposts at each end. Families still picnic on the grass at night. People in Iran have a rhyming saying about this city. In Persian it goes: Esfahan, nesf-e jahan. Isfahan is half the world.
screen: `A SQUARE THE SIZE OF A TOWN.` → `A PALACE, A BAZAAR, BLUE MOSQUES.` → `ESFAHAN, NESF-E JAHAN.`

segments.voice: Isfahan became the capital of the Safavid shahs, and under Shah Abbas it was rebuilt around this great square, called Naqsh-e Jahan, the image of the world. On the south side stands the Shah Mosque, now often called the Imam Mosque. Its gate faces the square. But walk through it and something odd happens: the building turns. The square runs one way; the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, runs another. So the architects bent the entrance, and the mosque behind it swings around to face Mecca. The square belongs to the city. The prayer hall belongs to the qibla. On the east side is a smaller mosque, named for Sheikh Lotfollah, a scholar. It has no minarets and no great courtyard. Inside is one room under a dome, and the tiles climb the dome in a pattern that narrows toward a center, with light from small windows falling across them. And the tiles. Blue, turquoise, yellow, white, cut and fitted, or painted and fired, covering walls, arches, domes. There are Qur'an verses written in tall letters, and flowers, and vines, and patterns that repeat, rather than pictures of people or animals. Why so much beauty in a prayer room? A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih Muslim, says that God is beautiful and loves beauty. And the Qur'an says that to God belong the east and the west, and wherever you turn, there is the face of God. A city that called itself half the world, and a prayer hall that turned away from the city to face one point. Half the world.
screen: `NAQSH-E JAHAN: THE IMAGE OF THE WORLD.` · `THE MOSQUE TURNS TO FACE MECCA.` · `A DOME WITH NO MINARETS.` · `GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.` · then, large: `HALF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at blue tiles. If you have a screen nearby, find one photo of the dome of the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque or the gate of the Shah Mosque in Isfahan. If not, look at anything blue near you: a mug, a sky, a shirt. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes move slowly from the edge toward the center, the way the pattern climbs the dome. Don't try to name everything. Notice where the pattern repeats and where it changes. If you pray, you can let the beauty turn you toward God. If you don't, simply let it be beautiful. The bell holds the time.
Isfahan. The Safavid capital, built around a vast square with a palace, a bazaar and blue-tiled mosques. Today's word.
Your line: half the world. Today, find one beautiful made thing on your way: a tiled floor, a carved door, a painted sign, and stop long enough to really see it. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

fork.setup: you're the architect. the shah's square runs one way. the qibla, toward Mecca, runs another. the mosque has to sit on the square. what do you do?
options: line the mosque up with the square and ignore the qibla.
face the gate to the square and turn the building toward Mecca.
build it somewhere else.
fork.reveal: the gate faces the square, and the entrance bends so the prayer hall faces Mecca. the square belongs to the city; the prayer hall belongs to the qibla.

original.note: Persian: half the world, from the saying Esfahan, nesf-e jahan.

trapdoor: what you thought: half the world is just a boast.
what it means: a rhyming Persian saying about a Safavid capital built around a vast square.
what a scholar hears: Naqsh-e Jahan, the image of the world, and a mosque gate that faces the city while the prayer hall turns toward Mecca.

989.title: Samarkand's Registan
989.hook: the Timurid square of madrasahs in Uzbekistan
989.howItsDone: Madrasahs are schools of Islamic learning where students study the Qur'an, hadith and law, traditionally living in rooms around a courtyard; the Registan's madrasahs are now visited as historic monuments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isfahan, and a mosque that turned away from the square to face Mecca. Your line was: half the world. What beautiful made thing stopped you? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

A tiled gateway, taller than the buildings around it. Across its arch, two great striped cats run, each chasing a white deer. Behind each cat rises a sun, and in the sun is a human face, calm, looking straight out at you. It is not a palace. It is not a picture gallery. It is the front of a school for studying the Qur'an and Islamic law. And it stands on one of the famous squares of Central Asia, in the old Silk Road city of Samarkand, in what is now Uzbekistan. The square has a modest name. Today: Samarkand's Registan.
screen: `CATS CHASING WHITE DEER.` → `A SUN WITH A HUMAN FACE.` → `ON THE FRONT OF A SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Registan, in Persian, is usually explained as the sandy place. It was an open ground in the middle of Samarkand, where people gathered for markets, announcements and public occasions. Samarkand was the capital of Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia whose campaigns left terrible destruction across many lands, and who also brought craftsmen from the cities he took to build his capital. His descendants, the Timurids, ruled after him, and some of them spent their wealth on learning. Around the sandy place, they and later rulers raised madrasahs, schools where students lived and studied. Ulugh Beg, Timur's grandson, built one of the madrasahs that face the square. Tomorrow's lesson is his. Later came the Sher-Dor, the one with the cats and the suns, and the Tilya-Kori, whose name speaks of gold, with a mosque inside covered in gilding. A madrasah is a courtyard ringed with small rooms, where students slept, read, copied and argued, with a teacher's lecture hall and a place to pray. The Qur'an's first revelation, as tradition tells it, begins with a command to read. In Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." And it goes on to speak of the Lord who taught by the pen. So a public square, once just sand, was ringed with schools. And the cats on the Sher-Dor? Mosques and madrasahs commonly use letters and patterns rather than pictures of living creatures, and some scholars disapproved of such pictures. The Sher-Dor's builders put them right on the gate. People still argue about what the suns and cats meant. The sandy place.
screen: `REGISTAN: THE SANDY PLACE.` · `TIMUR'S CITY, HIS GRANDSON'S SCHOOL.` · `A COURTYARD OF STUDENTS' ROOMS.` · `READ: IN THE NAME OF THY LORD.` · then, large: `THE SANDY PLACE.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the Registan. A photo of the square, or of the Sher-Dor gate with its cats and suns, will do if one is close at hand. Otherwise, picture an empty patch of sand in a city center, and then picture schools rising on its sides. Settle, and breathe. Look slowly. Find the gate, the domes, the tiles, the doors to the students' rooms. Think of one thing you are learning right now, however small. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. If you don't, simply hold your question. The bell holds the time.
Samarkand's Registan. The sandy place: an open square in Timur's capital, ringed by madrasahs where students lived and studied. Today's word.
Your line: the sandy place. Today, find one ordinary open space you pass, a lot, a park, a lobby, and wonder what could be built there for learning. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

fork.reveal: the Sher-Dor's builders put cats, deer and faced suns on the gate. people still argue about what they meant.

what it means: an open sandy square in Samarkand, ringed with madrasahs, schools where students lived and studied.
what a scholar hears: Ulugh Beg's madrasah facing the square, then the Sher-Dor with its cats and faced suns, a gate that breaks a common avoidance of images.

990.title: Ulugh Beg
990.hook: the ruler-astronomer whose observatory mapped the stars over Samarkand
990.howItsDone: Muslims time the daily prayers by the sun and the months of the Islamic calendar by the moon, and mosques and prayer apps today still use astronomical calculation to set prayer times and the direction of Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samarkand's Registan, a square of sand ringed with schools, and a gate with cats and faced suns. Your line was: the sandy place. Which open space did you notice? Day nine hundred ninety.

Steps lead down into a trench cut in a hill outside Samarkand. At the bottom, you stand between two long, curved walls of stone and brick, sweeping down into the earth like a slide made for a giant. Marks run along the curve. This is what survives of a great instrument, built so that astronomers could watch the sun, moon and stars cross the sky and measure exactly where they stood. For a long time the whole building was lost under the soil, until archaeologists dug it out. The man who built it was not a hired scientist. He ruled the city. Today: Ulugh Beg.
screen: `A CURVED TRENCH ON A HILL.` → `AN INSTRUMENT FOR THE SKY.` → `BUILT BY THE MAN WHO RULED.`

segments.voice: Ulugh Beg was a grandson of Timur, the conqueror whose capital was Samarkand. Where his grandfather was remembered for war, Ulugh Beg is remembered for study. He governed Samarkand and built the madrasah on the Registan you met yesterday, and he gathered mathematicians and astronomers around him. Then he built the observatory on the hill, with its great curved instrument set along the line from north to south. Night after night, his astronomers measured. Out of their work came tables of the stars: where each one sat in the sky, with tables of the sun, moon and planets. Astronomers in later centuries, in other lands, studied and copied them. Why would a Muslim ruler care so much about the sky? Partly because a Muslim day is shaped by it. The daily prayers follow the sun. The months follow the moon. The direction of prayer, toward Mecca, has to be worked out from wherever you stand. Astronomy served all of that. And the Qur'an itself points upward. It says God appointed the stars so that people could find their way by them in the darkness of land and sea, and that the moon was measured out in stages so people could know the number of the years and the reckoning of time. The Qur'an calls such things signs, and an astronomer measuring them was working inside that picture of the sky. His story ends hard. In a struggle over power, his own son turned against him, and Ulugh Beg was killed. Later the observatory was ruined and buried, and the curved trench waited in the earth. The astronomer king.
screen: `TIMUR'S GRANDSON, REMEMBERED FOR STUDY.` · `AN OBSERVATORY ON THE HILL.` · `PRAYER FOLLOWS THE SUN AND MOON.` · `STARS TO FIND YOUR WAY BY.` · then, large: `THE ASTRONOMER KING.`

segments.voice: The practice: count the stars you can see. If it's dark where you are, step outside or go to a window. If it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the last night sky you saw clearly. Settle, and breathe. Count slowly, one star at a time, not to get a number, but to notice each one. When you lose count, start again. Notice the brightest one and where it sits. If you pray, you can let each star be a sign you thank God for. If you don't, simply look. The bell holds the time.
Ulugh Beg. Timur's grandson, who ruled Samarkand, built an observatory on a hill, and with his astronomers made tables of the stars. Today's word.
Your line: the astronomer king. Tonight, look up once before you sleep, find one star or the moon, and remember where it was. Tomorrow night, check if it moved. Day nine hundred ninety.

to know the reckoning of time

991.title: Sufi saints of India
991.hook: Mu'in al-Din Chishti in Ajmer and Nizam al-Din in Delhi, whose shrines draw people of all faiths
991.howItsDone: At Sufi shrines (dargahs) in South Asia, visitors offer flowers and cloth, listen to qawwali, and receive food cooked in large pots and served to all, while other Muslims, citing the teaching that prayer belongs to God alone, avoid shrine customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ulugh Beg, the ruler who built an observatory and read the stars as signs. Your line was: the astronomer king. Did you find a star or the moon before you slept? Day nine hundred ninety-one.

Thursday evening in Delhi. A narrow lane, so packed you move with the crowd, past stalls selling rose petals, sheets of embroidered cloth, sweets and prayer caps. At the end, a courtyard of white marble and a tomb under a dome. Men and women in head coverings sit on the floor. Some are Muslims. Some are Hindus, some Sikhs, some Christians, some just curious. Then the singers start: a harmonium, hand drums, voices rising and falling in poems about longing for God. This is the shrine of a Sufi saint who died long ago, and people still gather around his grave. Today: Sufi saints of India.
screen: `A PACKED LANE OF ROSE PETALS.` → `A MARBLE COURTYARD AND A TOMB.` → `PEOPLE OF EVERY FAITH, SINGING.`

segments.voice: Two names lead the way. Mu'in al-Din Chishti came to India from the lands to the west and settled in Ajmer, in Rajasthan. Nizam al-Din Awliya taught later in Delhi, in the same Sufi line, the Chishti order. Both are remembered not for armies or palaces but for open doors. Tradition says Nizam al-Din's lodge fed visitors all day long, rich or poor, Muslim or not, and that he gave away what came to him rather than keep it. At Ajmer today, huge cooking pots are filled and the food is served to whoever comes. Pilgrims call Mu'in al-Din Gharib Nawaz, the friend of the poor. Why food? The Qur'an praises those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for love of God. In Pickthall's translation, they say: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Nizam al-Din's student was the poet Amir Khusrau, remembered for songs still sung at these shrines, and he is buried near his teacher. The singing in that Delhi courtyard, qawwali, is linked to that circle. Muslims do not all see these shrines the same way. Some treasure the visit, the music and the blessing of a holy person's memory. Others, pointing to the Prophet's teaching that prayer belongs to God alone, avoid praying at graves and question the music. Both are Muslims, reading the same sources. And at the shrines, the pots are still full, and the kitchen is still open. The open kitchen.
screen: `AJMER AND DELHI.` · `THE FRIEND OF THE POOR.` · `WE FEED YOU FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH.` · `MUSLIMS SEE SHRINES DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `THE OPEN KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: serve food to all comers, beginning in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Think about the next meal you'll share or make. Who might you feed who isn't usually at your table? A neighbor living alone. A coworker who eats at their desk. A friend going through a hard week. A stranger, through a food bank. Picture handing them a plate, and wanting nothing back, not even thanks. If you pray, you can ask that the food be a blessing. If you don't, simply choose who it will be. The bell holds the time.
Chishti. The Sufi order of teachers like Mu'in al-Din in Ajmer and Nizam al-Din in Delhi, whose shrines feed and welcome people of every faith. Today's word.
Your line: the open kitchen. Today, feed one person you wouldn't usually feed: share a snack, buy a coffee, set an extra plate, and ask for nothing back. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: The Mughals
992.hook: Babur, Akbar and their successors rule much of South Asia
992.howItsDone: Mughal mosques, tombs and gardens in India and Pakistan, such as the Jama Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, are still places of prayer and visiting today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sufi saints of India, and shrines in Ajmer and Delhi where the cooking pots feed whoever comes. Your line was: the open kitchen. Who did you feed? Day nine hundred ninety-two.

A king is writing his diary, and he is homesick. He has just won a great battle and taken Delhi and Agra. Treasure, elephants, a new country. And what does he complain about? The melons. In his own memoir, he grumbles that his new land has no good melons and grapes, no cold running water, no proper gardens laid out in order. He misses the orchards of the valley where he grew up, far to the north in Central Asia. So, the memoir says, he soon starts digging channels and planting a garden. The king's name was Babur, and his family would rule much of South Asia. Today: the Mughals.
screen: `A HOMESICK KING'S DIARY.` → `NO GOOD MELONS HERE.` → `HE PLANTS A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Babur was a descendant of Timur, the same family line as Ulugh Beg of Samarkand. He lost his own small kingdom in Central Asia, came south through Kabul, and won his way into India. His memoir, written in his Turkic mother tongue, is frank: battles, friendships, regrets, his drinking and his giving it up, and gardens everywhere. The Mughal garden became a signature: beds divided by water channels, with a pool or a pavilion at the center. The Qur'an pictures paradise as gardens with water. In Pickthall's translation: "Gardens underneath which rivers flow." Many historians read a walled Mughal garden with running water as a small picture of that promise. Babur's grandson was Akbar. He built a new city at Fatehpur Sikri, and in it a hall where he invited scholars to debate: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, and Jesuit priests from Portuguese Goa. He listened, asked questions, and let them argue in front of him. Some Muslim scholars of his court admired this, and some objected strongly, and historians still argue about what Akbar himself came to believe. After Akbar came his son Jahangir, then Shah Jahan, then Aurangzeb, each with his own story, and the empire's courts filled with Persian poetry, painting, music and buildings of red sandstone and white marble. Babur's homesick garden had grown into an empire. The Mughals.
screen: `BABUR, TIMUR'S DESCENDANT.` · `GARDENS WITH RIVERS FLOWING.` · `AKBAR'S HALL OF DEBATE.` · `PAINTING, POETRY, MARBLE.` · then, large: `THE MUGHALS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about one Mughal city. Choose one: Agra, with its red fort by the river; Delhi, with its great mosque; Lahore, with its gardens; or Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's city of debate. Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself walking into it, the way Babur walked into a new land. What would you look for first? Water? A garden? A mosque? A market? Later today, if you have a few minutes, look up one picture of it. If you pray, you can remember the people who prayed there. If you don't, simply let yourself be curious. The bell holds the time.
The Mughals. The dynasty of Babur and Akbar and their successors, who ruled much of South Asia and filled it with gardens, poetry and marble. Today's word.
Your line: he missed the melons. Today, if you're missing somewhere, do what Babur did: plant something, even a single herb in a cup, and let it grow where you are. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: The Taj Mahal
993.hook: Shah Jahan's tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, framed with Qur'an verses
993.howItsDone: Muslims pray for the dead and visit graves to remember them; the mosque beside the Taj Mahal is still used for Friday prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mughals: Babur's homesick garden, Akbar's hall of debate. Your line was: he missed the melons. Did you plant anything where you are? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

Everything is in pairs. Walk through the great gate and the garden opens in front of you, split by a long channel of water that holds the white dome upside down. Minarets stand at each corner of the platform, matched. To the left of the tomb, a red sandstone mosque; to the right, a building that copies it exactly, so the view stays balanced. Inside, under the dome, two marble cenotaphs lie side by side. And that is where the balance breaks. One sits at the exact center. The other is pushed to the side, as if it arrived later and squeezed in. It did. Today: the Taj Mahal.
screen: `A DOME IN THE WATER.` → `EVERYTHING MATCHED.` → `ONE TOMB OFF-CENTER.`

segments.voice: The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife, the empress known by the title “Mumtaz Mahal”, who died while he was emperor. The center of the whole design belongs to her. When Shah Jahan himself died, he was laid beside her, and his tomb is the one off-center, breaking the balance. People call it a monument to love, and it is. But walk closer and the white marble is framed with writing. Black stone letters set into the marble, framing the arches and the gate: verses from the Qur'an. The calligrapher, Amanat Khan, signed his work, and the letters are said to grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they look the same size all the way up. Among the verses on the great gate, guides point to the end of the surah called al-Fajr, the Dawn. In Pickthall's translation: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" And then: enter among My servants, enter My garden. So a visitor walks through words about a soul returning to God, into a garden with water, toward a grave. The love story is real. But the building also speaks about death, judgment and paradise. The Taj holds two questions in white stone: how to honor the one you've lost, and where the soul goes next. A tomb for love.
screen: `A TOMB FOR AN EMPRESS.` · `SHAH JAHAN, OFF-CENTER.` · `LETTERS THAT GROW AS THEY CLIMB.` · `RETURN UNTO THY LORD.` · then, large: `A TOMB FOR LOVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a love that's gone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you loved who has died, or a love that ended, or a person who moved far away. Let their face come. Let one ordinary memory come: a voice, a kitchen, a joke. You don't have to build anything. Just hold them for a minute, the way the garden holds the tomb at its center. If grief comes, let it. If you pray, you can pray for them, as Muslims pray for their dead. If you don't, simply say their name. The bell holds the time.
Mumtaz Mahal. The empress for whom Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra, white marble framed with Qur'an verses about the soul returning to God. Today's word.
Your line: a tomb for love. Today, do one small thing to honor someone you've lost: say their name aloud, cook their dish, or tell someone a story about them. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh
994.hook: two brothers: one a pious, contested emperor, the other a mystic who studied Hindu scriptures, with a hard history between them
994.howItsDone: Muslims remember Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh in different ways: some honor Aurangzeb's personal piety and his sponsorship of Islamic law, some honor Dara Shikoh's Sufi search, and historians continue to debate both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Taj Mahal: a tomb for love, framed with verses about the soul returning to its Lord. Your line was: a tomb for love. Whose name did you say aloud? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

Shah Jahan, the man who built the Taj, has sons. Two of them matter today. The elder, Dara Shikoh, is his father's favorite, a scholar who keeps company with Sufis and with Hindu holy men. The younger, Aurangzeb, is a soldier and governor, serious, devout, careful with every prayer. When their father falls ill, the brothers go to war with each other for the throne. Only one of them will live. And long afterward, people will still argue about both brothers, and about what India would have been if the other had won. Today: Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh.
screen: `SHAH JAHAN'S SONS.` → `A SCHOLAR AND A SOLDIER.` → `A WAR FOR THE THRONE.`

segments.voice: Dara Shikoh followed the Qadiri Sufi path. He believed that seekers in different traditions were reaching toward the same truth, and he went looking for it. He worked with Hindu scholars to translate the Upanishads, Hindu scriptures, into Persian. And he wrote a short book comparing Sufi and Hindu terms, called Majma al-Bahrayn, the meeting place of the two seas. The title comes from the Qur'an. In the story of Moses seeking a wise servant of God, Moses says, in Pickthall's translation: "I will not give up until I reach the point where the two rivers meet." Aurangzeb won the war. Dara was captured, brought through Delhi in disgrace, and judged by scholars who said his writings had left Islam. He was put to death. Their father spent his last years confined in the fort at Agra. That is the hard history. And Aurangzeb? His long reign is remembered in more than one way. Some Muslims remember him as a deeply pious ruler, who, tradition says, copied the Qur'an and sewed prayer caps to pay for his own needs, and who sponsored a great collection of Islamic law. Others, among them Hindus and Sikhs, remember the tax he restored on non-Muslims and the temples destroyed under his rule. Historians still argue about how to weigh it all. Two brothers. One read across traditions looking for where the waters meet. One held tightly to the law as he understood it. Two brothers, two paths.

segments.voice: The practice: think about brothers who disagree, or sisters, or friends. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two people you love who see faith or life very differently. Maybe one of them is you. Don't decide who's right. Notice what each one is holding onto, and what they're afraid of losing. Then think about this week's road: Isfahan's turning mosque, the sandy place in Samarkand, the astronomer king, the open kitchen, Babur's garden, the Taj. If you pray, you can pray for the people you love who disagree. If you don't, simply hold them both. The bell holds the time.
Dara Shikoh, the scholar-prince who studied with Sufis and Hindu holy men, translated the Upanishads, and was put to death by his brother Aurangzeb. Today's word.

Your line: two brothers, two paths. That closes Persia, the Turks and the great empires. Tomorrow the road turns east, to Southeast Asia. Today, ask one person you disagree with a real question, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred ninety-four.
